title: How to Prepare for Your Funding Specialist Call
seo_title: How to Prepare for Your Funding Specialist Call
meta_description: Get more from your funding conversation. Learn what to gather, which numbers to know and what to ask your funding specialist before you commit to anything.
keywords: what to bring to a funding call
how to talk to a funder
dek: A few minutes of preparation turns a generic phone call into a focused conversation about offers that fit.
intro: The call with a funding specialist is where an application becomes a plan. It is also where owners most often leave value on the table, either because they did not have a number handy, or because they felt rushed and skipped the questions they cared about. Neither is the specialist's fault. A busy owner is simply pulled back to the shop floor before the call has finished.

A little preparation changes that. When you can state what you need, how you will repay it and what you are comparing against, the specialist can narrow the field quickly and you can leave with real clarity. This guide walks through what to settle before the call, what to have in front of you and the questions worth asking.

sections.h2: Decide what the money is for
paragraphs: The more specific the purpose, the better the match. Buying a $28,000 piece of equipment that you will use for years is a different need from covering a seasonal gap in March, and they point toward different products. Equipment financing, a line of credit, a term loan and a merchant cash advance each handle cash flow differently.

Write the purpose in one sentence and the amount you think you need in another. If you are unsure, name a range and what drives it. Then ask yourself what the money should produce, because an owner who can articulate the return is easier to match with the right structure.
You do not need to memorize your books, but a handful of figures should be on the tip of your tongue. Funding partners tend to review the same basics, and having them ready shortens the call.

If you are not sure of a figure, say so and give a range. An honest estimate is more useful to a specialist than a confident guess that your bank statements will contradict. Rounding is fine; the statements will fill in the rest.
bullets: Average monthly deposits over the last three to six months, and whether they are seasonal.
Time in business and your legal business name and entity type.
Existing funding obligations, including balances and daily or weekly payments.
Your largest monthly fixed costs: rent, payroll, loan payments, insurance.
Any liens, judgments or recent bankruptcies, stated honestly.

paragraphs: Typical requests include recent business bank statements, a voided check or account details, a government ID and sometimes a tax return or a processing statement. Requirements vary by funding partner and by amount, but gathering these ahead of time keeps the process moving.

If you take card payments, your merchant statements show your processing volume and fees. Fidelity Funding's card-processing partner, PayPilot by MCCPS, can also review a statement and quote pricing, which is worth asking about on the call if you suspect you are overpaying.
Treat the call as an interview. A good specialist welcomes direct questions and answers them plainly. Some that are worth asking:
steps: Which funding partners will review my file, and what product does each offer?
What is the total payback or total cost on each offer, not just the rate?
How are payments collected, how often, and what happens in a slow week?
Are there origination fees, early payoff terms or a personal guarantee?
What happens next, and how long until I see funds if I accept?

sections.h2: Say the hard parts out loud
paragraphs: If there is a blemish in your file, such as a tax lien, a prior default, an overdraft stretch or an existing advance, mention it. Specialists have heard all of it, and an honest picture lets them route you toward partners who will actually review the file. Surprises discovered in underwriting cost you days.

The same goes for your timeline. If you need funds by Friday, say so. If you are only exploring, say that too. Fidelity Funding's process is built around a short application and a soft credit pull for the initial review, so there is no pressure to commit while you are learning what the market may offer.

It also helps to decide your walk-away point. Before the call, think about the largest daily or weekly payment you could carry in your slowest month, and the total payback beyond which the funding would not be worth it. Having those limits in mind keeps a persuasive conversation from steering you past them.

Write down the offers discussed, including the amount, total payback, payment schedule and fees. Do not accept something you cannot explain back in your own words. If a figure was stated verbally, ask for it in writing, and read any agreement in full before signing. For a legal or tax question, loop in your attorney or CPA.

Finally, test the payment against reality. Take the weekly or daily payment, divide your typical weekly deposits by it, and ask whether the business can absorb it in its slowest month. Approval, pricing and timing vary by funding partner and underwriting, so none of this is a guarantee, but a prepared owner reaches a better decision faster.

key_takeaways: Define the purpose and amount before the call.
Have deposits, obligations and time in business at your fingertips.
Gather bank statements and ID ahead of time.
Ask about total payback, fees, payment mechanics and personal guarantees.
Disclose blemishes early and get offers in writing.

faq.q: What should I have ready for a funding call?
faq.a: Know your average monthly deposits, time in business, existing obligations and the purpose and amount you need. Have recent bank statements and an ID available. Requirements vary by funding partner, but being prepared helps your specialist narrow the options and respond more quickly.

faq.q: How long does a call with a funding specialist take?
faq.a: It varies, but many are a short conversation focused on your goals and numbers. A specialist reviews options with you and may follow up with offers and document requests. Preparing ahead can shorten it, and you are free to take time to consider any offer.

faq.q: Do I need to know exactly how much I need?
faq.a: A precise number helps, but a range with a clear reason is fine. Your specialist can help you size a request to your deposits and repayment ability. Asking for far more than the business can comfortably repay tends to make the offers worse, not better.

faq.q: Will the call affect my credit?
faq.a: At Fidelity Funding, the initial review uses a soft credit pull, which does not impact your score. If you choose to move forward with a specific funding partner, a different credit check may be involved, and your specialist can explain what to expect.

faq.q: Should I take an offer on the first call?
faq.a: There is no need to rush. Review the total payback, payment schedule, fees and any guarantees, and compare offers. Ask for terms in writing and take time to run the numbers with your CPA or advisor if you want a second opinion.
